To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the dynamics of host parasite interactions is sensitive to the presence of three types of biological processes: (i) host reproductive suppression, (ii) parasite reproduction within the host and (iii) time delays in parasite development or parasite transmission.

the dynamics of a host-parasite interaction is strongly dependent on the relative rates of host and parasite growth and that the dynamics is also dependent on the relative magnitude of host and parasite population sizes.

The stability of a host population in the presence of a parasite is dependent upon the relative magnitudes of the parasite induced reduction in the host population growth rate, the parasite induced increase in the host population death rate, and the parasite reproduction and transmission rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of mathematical models which describe the dynamics of host parasite interactions in terms of the biological and environmental factors which influence them.

the development and analysis of models of host-parasite population interactions and the application of these to the analysis of field and laboratory studies of host-parasitoid and host-microparasite associations.
the dynamical behaviour and regulation of population interactions between hosts and parasites.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence for parasite induced regulation of host population growth in natural situations is not convincing, and is probably not strong.
the importance of parasites as regulators of host populations remains an open question.
the role of parasitic species in host population regulation is not well understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
host parasite population interactions are not generally stable and that the dynamics of such interactions are strongly influenced by the biological processes involved in host parasite interactions.
the regulation of host population growth by parasite species is a common phenomenon, but one whose importance is likely to be highly variable.
the stability of a host-parasite system is a function of the reproductive and mortality characteristics of both the host and parasite species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the regulation of host population size by parasite species may be a more important factor in host population dynamics than is generally recognized.
the regulation of host populations by their parasitoids may be more common than is currently believed.
parasites can have a stabilizing or a destabilizing influence, depending on the details of their life history and the nature of the host-parasite interaction.
